Imports Killing the SA Chicken Industry

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
1000 lose jobs as the chicken South African Chicken Industry collapses because of cheap imports flooding the market

Summary:
South Africa’s poultry industry, the largest in Africa, is in severe crisis and facing major job losses as a result of the dumping of cheap chicken imports from mainly Brazil and the United States. Rainbow Chickens, one of SA’s biggest producers, is selling 31 of its 51 KwaZulu Natal farms at Hammarsdale and retrenching 1 350 workers.
In Polokwane, Limpopo, the 38-year-old family-owned Mike’s Chickens has closed down, with more than a thousand jobs lost. Country Birds, who operate in the Free State and North West and who are the SA’s third biggest chicken producer after Astral Foods (which operates in Mpumalanga, Gauteng, the Western Cape and KZN) and Rainbow, is retrenching 1 500 workers.
The chief executive of the SA Poultry Association, Kevin Lovell, says about 540 000 tons of chicken were imported last year – more than is produced annually by SA’s biggest producer, Astral Foods.



Further information:
Scott Pitman, managing director of RCL Foods (Rainbow Chickens), was quoted this week as saying he no longer knew what to do to save jobs. “Letting 1 350 people go at the end of the month will be the saddest day in my career. How do you get rid of people who have given you loyal service, some as long as 40 years?” he asked. He said government was doing nothing to tighten import controls on frozen chicken, and the EU and Brazil, especially, were capitalising on this with large-scale dumping, especially of thighs and drumsticks (“brown portions”) as the consumer preference in Europe was for breast meat (“white portions”).
“Our company’s troubles could end and jobs saved overnight if the government placed tighter regulations on imports,” Pitman was quoted as saying. “If government doesn’t intervene soon, we will cut more jobs.”
Lovell said “the Ghanaian poultry industry has collapsed because of EU dumping. This is a form of post-colonial oppression.”

Press Release:


Chicken Industry on a Knife Edge
The South African poultry industry is in dire crisis and thousands of workers stand to lose their jobs as local production faces collapse. Role players blame cheap chicken imports from Brazil and the United States for flooding the market, leaving local producers unable to compete. Government has intervened and is working with poultry producers to address the industry’s challenges, but is it too little too late? Carte Blanche asks if tighter import regulations and so-called ‘anti-dumping measures’ will safeguard local production?


Script:


Link: Rainbow Chickens has been in Hammersdale since 1963. At full capacity the plant employs 2700 people but in just two weeks that figure will be halved, and that doesn’t sound like a very high number but as the largest employer in this area it’s going to have devastating consequences for this community
Script: Busiswe Mgoba has worked at Rainbow Chickens for the last 32 years, since she left school, her wage supports 12 people.
Busiswe “I don’t know my head is spinning I don’t know I didn’t think that a company as big as this one will just end like a tuck shop
Script: Lindelani Khwela is losing his job after 10 years, he supports 8 people
Lindelani “At this moment I am confused. I was afraid to even inform my wife
Script: Scott Pittman head of Rainbow Chickens was in a remote part of Kenya this week and sent us this comment
Scott: “We have deliberately avoided completely closing Hammersdale although obviously that was one of our considerations and so what we have done instead is cut the number of shifts from 2 down to one and effectively halved the production of Hammersdale”
Link: RCL foods the company behind the Rainbow Brand are the countries 2nd largest poultry producers but just last month 30 000 tons of imported chicken were brought into the country now that is more than they make in a month and as a consequence 31 out of 51 farms in the KZN region alone will face closure 1000s of jobs will be lost
Script: This community still has not recovered from the collapse of the textile industry. The unemployment rate sits at 67%, says community activist Nathi Mkhize
Bongani: It’s a bit of a disaster isn’t it?
Nathi “Yes in fact it is a catastrophe from where we are sitting. Many people who are going to be affected and then they are going to be dependent on the local councillor and government and then the government is not in a position to sufficiently provide for everyone
Script: Last year South Africa imported more chicken products into the country than ever before, 540 000 tons which is roughly 45% of the local market, coupled with the increased cost of feed due to the drought, our Poultry industry is on its knees.
Kevin Lovell “Where we are as an industry is at the textile type tipping point when the banks stop financing the companies they will shut very quickly so it’s very hard for me to know when the banks will shut down but when they do shut down I could easily see between 12 and 25 000 jobs disappearing
Script: Kevin Lovell CEO of the South African Poultry Association is also on the international poultry council
Kevin Lovell “When we became a democracy we needed to reengage with the world and establish new trading relationships on a new basis and we somewhat naively thought our trading partners would be decent. But in trade decency doesn’t exist trade is about money and money doesn’t have much decency behind it. So when you import chicken for every 10 000 tons of chicken meat and by that I mean stuff that looks like a chicken we lose just over 1 000 direct and indirect jobs gone never get them back we are the fall over and die but I can’t tell you when
Script: European and America markets consume mainly chicken breasts and are left with the rest of the bird to dispose of, so they freeze the offcuts and export it to the rest of the developing world at below local production costs
Chris “They recover the full cost of the production of the bird just in the breast meat, we don’t have that luxury in SA to charge R140 a kg for white breast meat
Script: Chris Schutter, CEO of Astral foods the largest producer in the country says they are down 50% on last year’s figures.
Chris “When we negotiated the AGOA agreement - lets have fair play bring a whole bird here compete with us on like for like and we are prepared to accept that don’t just bring the parts you can’t sell there and force your negative eating habits onto our industry or our population, because that is what is harming us it is not the import of poultry it’s the import of certain products below the production cost of what they can produce in their back yard in the EU
Script: The SA poultry industry has been accused of inefficiencies yet they rated 5th in the world despite high feed costs. Independent Dutch studies found that on a bird to bird basis our production is 50% cheaper than the EU and we consume 94% of the bird. Of the 540 000 tons imported last year only 3% is actual chicken pieces, the rest are offcuts and chicken paste.
Bongani: Surely there are mechanism trade restraints where dumping can be targeted
Kevin Lowell “I know this is a crass way to describe something it, in trade law you first have to be raped before you can ask for protection, so you first have to suffer harm because it is one of the tests of dumping …before you can lodge a successful action. Dumping is also an action against companies not countries so you have to wait to be harmed. Currently there are 10 of the 28 European countries that can export to SA, so you have to wait for all 10 of those countries to harm you… before you can lodge an action and it can take up to 18 months for it to be resolved by which time you are going downhill”
Script: Minister of Trade and Industry Rob Davies says they are acutely aware of crisis
Rob Davies’ “I signed off in the middle of December a provisional Safeguard duty of 13.9 percent. Now I am aware that the industry wants this to be higher, but at the time I was faced with the option because we don’t set the tariffs as ministers, we go through recommendations coming from the International Trade Administration Commission, and I was faced with the choice of doing what I did, which was to say ‘go back and look at a final duty, but let me sign off on the provisional duty to at least put something in place’.
Chris “I think the currency plays a major role in that 13.9% is the equivalence of 17 Euro cents or 12 pence so it’s ridiculous to think that small amount is going to deter them of disposing of their waste in our country.
Scott “SA is not allowed to export chicken to virtually anywhere in the world. In South America they say we don’t approve your abattoirs therefore you can’t export chicken to us although we have world class abattoirs. In North America they say your ostriches have got bird flu and therefore you can’t export chicken to us although we have never had bird flu in our chicken flocks ever. In Europe they say the same and in Australia they just ban imports of poultry. And places like Russia, Nigeria and Kenya and most of our African neighbours will say you can’t export your chicken to us because we are protecting our local industries. We need a technical barrier which are called phyto sanitary barriers and we need out Government to implement whatever duties are necessary to help at least I the short term but also in the longer term
Link: As with many issues in SA it is the poorest of the poor who are hardest hit with this issue this is typical of frozen chicken pieces sold at the lower end of the retail market there is nothing about country of origin if it’s been defrosted and refrozen and there is not even a sell by date its basically. It’s the wild wild west
Bongai: Do we know when we are buying imported meat
Kevin 02 20 53 “If you go to the delicatessen counters and its sold either raw or frozen you will not know where it comes from if you buy from catering companies you have no idea where it comes from if you go to a fast food in SA it is almost certainly local chicken.
Link: as picturesque as it seems this is a struggling community so who would argue against cheaper proteins yet it is that affordable meat that is hurting employment in this community it’s a horrible catch 22
Rob Davies “We don’t think that food security can be created on a sustainable and long term basis by importing products from elsewhere. We don’t feel the playing fields is level or fair, and at the same time we have our arms twisted to open up our markets for the brown meat so we are operating within a terrain that is not of our choosing and it is quite a difficult terrain to negotiate
Script: The Food and Allied Workers Union Katishi Masemola says 8000 direct and indirect jobs have already been lost
Katishi Masemola “If there was to be a fair competition between ourselves and Europe in other words that Europe doesn’t place technical barriers to trade for our chicken products we can actually add 20 000 to 25 000 jobs
Script: Minister Davies has called a meeting for early next week with all industry players
Rob Davies “We will be looking at a broader package than just the import issues and deal with the trade issues, not just the issue of imports coming into South Africa but also of opening up new markets abroad, because for example in the United Arab Emirates we have recently secured the removal of all the sanitary and phyto sanitary matters which means that that market is effectively open
Chris “It’s a bit little too late, we are already in the process of cutting back, reducing jobs reducing shifts I can’t reverse that now that planning was done that conversation should have taken place a number of months ago when we warned the government
Kevin “If we didn’t import anything we would probably be able to create around 50 000 direct and indirect jobs so 5% of the SA jobs target sits with the import problem if we add export we can probably add another 40 – 50 000 jobs
Bongani’ “So given the crisis will you then still push for higher increases as far as wages are concerned
Katishi Masemola “We will be sensitive to what the employers are able to afford but we don’t want them to use an excuse of the crisis in order to give next to nothing to the employees
Busisiwe “It is so painful I had planned to do a lot of things a lot of things do while working at Rainbow. I thought when I don’t have energy anymore to work my children will come and work in this firm and support me.

Rainbow Chickens, one of SA’s biggest producers, is selling 31 of its 51 KwaZulu Natal farms at Hammarsdale and retrenching 1 350 workers. In Polokwane, Limpopo, the 38-year-old family-owned Mike’s Chickens has closed down, with more than a thousand jobs lost. Country Birds, who operate in the Free State and North West and who are the SA’s third biggest chicken producer after Astral Foods (which operates in Mpumalanga, Gauteng, the Western Cape and KZN) and Rainbow, is retrenching 1 500 workers. The chief executive of the SA Poultry Association, Kevin Lovell, says about 540 000 tons of chicken were imported last year – more than is produced annually by SA’s biggest producer, Astral Foods.
metadata.Further information: Scott Pitman, managing director of RCL Foods (Rainbow Chickens), was quoted this week as saying he no longer knew what to do to save jobs. “Letting 1 350 people go at the end of the month will be the saddest day in my career. How do you get rid of people who have given you loyal service, some as long as 40 years?” he asked. He said government was doing nothing to tighten import controls on frozen chicken, and the EU and Brazil, especially, were capitalising on this with large-scale dumping, especially of thighs and drumsticks (“brown portions”) as the consumer preference in Europe was for breast meat (“white portions”). “Our company’s troubles could end and jobs saved overnight if the government placed tighter regulations on imports,” Pitman was quoted as saying. “If government doesn’t intervene soon, we will cut more jobs.” Lovell said “the Ghanaian poultry industry has collapsed because of EU dumping. This is a form of post-colonial oppression.”
